prompt.context: Our client, FC Limited (Fine China Limited), manufactures sets of fine china (plates, tea cups, etc.). They only sell the china in sets — never as individual pieces — at $1,500 per set. Excess or lack of demand has never been a problem for FC; they sell 10,000 sets per year. The company was started 50 years ago and has been successful and profitable throughout its history. However, in the last 7 years a key competitor recently entered the industry. FC has recently learned that the competitor has at least 50% higher margins and would like to match or exceed its results.
prompt.question: Question 1: Why are FC's profit margins not as good as the new competitor's? How do you propose FC fix this problem? Question 2: Given the issues and recommendations from Question 1, how can FC cut costs, and what are the new expected profit margins?

clarifying_info.q: What are FC's sales volumes and pricing?
clarifying_info.a: FC sells exactly 10,000 sets per year at $1,500 per set. This volume is not expected to change.

clarifying_info.q: Is this a revenue problem or a cost problem?
clarifying_info.a: Revenue is stable; this is not a revenue generation issue. The problem is on the cost side.

clarifying_info.q: How do raw material costs compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Raw material costs (porcelain clay) are in-line with or less than competitors.

clarifying_info.q: How does manufacturing compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Manufacturing takes place at FC's North Carolina headquarters and is efficient; costs are slightly lower than competitors.

clarifying_info.q: What does FC's distribution network look like?
clarifying_info.a: FC has 6 warehouses: 2 in North Carolina, 2 in Ohio, and 2 in Southern California. China is manufactured in North Carolina and then shipped to regional warehouses for quicker delivery to retailers when orders are placed.

clarifying_info.q: How is the china sold — through which channels?
clarifying_info.a: The china is sold only as a set through upscale retail stores such as Neiman Marcus and Saks Fifth Avenue. Retailers do not hold inventory; they have one display set. Customers place orders for next-day pick-up from the store, or occasionally a salesperson makes a personal home delivery.

clarifying_info.q: What shipping method does FC use?
clarifying_info.a: When the company started, they used railroads. In the last 30 years they switched to trucks for transportation from the manufacturing plant to the warehouses. Delivery to stores requires 'white glove service' — no damage or sloppiness permitted.

clarifying_info.q: How does the key competitor operate?
clarifying_info.a: The competitor is located in Tennessee (Memphis). It has one warehouse and uses FedEx from its manufacturing site to ship directly to retailers; it also offers next-day delivery.

clarifying_info.q: What is white glove shipping cost if we switch carriers?
clarifying_info.a: Common carrier white glove service costs $150 per set shipped.

clarifying_info.q: How should we think about fixed cost allocation across facilities?
clarifying_info.a: A good proxy is square footage. The factory is twice the size of the average warehouse.

clarifying_info.q: What is FC's pricing vs. competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Pricing is in-line with or slightly higher than competitors. FC's price will not change.

exhibits.title: Fine China, Ltd — Income Statement (Interviewer Reference)
exhibits.shows: A two-column income statement showing the current cost structure and a proposed new income statement after cost reductions. Each cost line shows its percentage of total costs and the expected percentage reduction.
exhibits.data: Revenue: 10,000 sets x $1,500 = $15,000,000; Total Costs (given): $12,000,000; Cost breakdown: Raw Materials 20% ($2,400,000), Fixed Overhead 40% ($4,800,000), Labor 20% ($2,400,000), Shipping 10% ($1,200,000), Inventory Costs 10% ($1,200,000); Current Profit Margin: 20%

framework: Profitability lens: Revenue vs. Cost — confirm revenue is stable, then drill into cost structure
Value Chain / Supply Chain lens: trace raw materials → manufacturing → warehousing → distribution → retailer → customer
Identify where FC's cost structure diverges from the competitor's (distribution warehouses are the crux)
Compare FC's hub-and-spoke warehouse model to the competitor's single-warehouse + FedEx direct model
Quantify the cost savings from consolidating warehouses and switching to overnight carrier
Recalculate profit margin after cost changes

questions.prompt: Question 1: Why are FC's margins lower than the competitor's, and what should FC do?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate quickly recognizes this is both a profitability AND supply chain case. Walking the value chain reveals that raw materials and manufacturing are fine; the problem is distribution. FC runs 6 warehouses to achieve next-day delivery, while the competitor achieves the same service level from one warehouse using FedEx overnight. FC should eliminate most of its warehouses and shift to FedEx/UPS overnight shipping directly to retailers. The increased per-shipment cost is more than offset by elimination of warehouse fixed overhead, labor, and inventory carrying costs.

questions.prompt: Question 2a: Derive the current income statement. What is FC's current profit margin?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate revenue from given data, then as they name each cost category the interviewer reveals the percentage. Candidate should then compute profit and margin. Strong answer: revenue = $15M, total costs = $12M (given), profit = $3M, margin = 20%. The candidate should also show intuition about WHY each cost bucket is large (e.g., fixed overhead is 40% because of 6 warehouses).

math.setup: Revenue = 10,000 sets x $1,500/set. Total costs are given as $12,000,000. Profit = Revenue - Costs. Margin = Profit / Revenue.

questions.prompt: Question 2b: Given FC will eliminate most warehouse space, identify which cost lines change and calculate the new profit margin.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify each affected cost line and articulate WHY it changes. Raw materials stay the same (same production volume). Fixed overhead drops 50% (eliminate 4 of 6 warehouses, keep some NC capacity). Labor drops 25% (fewer workers loading/unloading at warehouses). Shipping increases 25% (FedEx overnight is more expensive than trucks per shipment). Inventory costs drop 50% (less stock sitting in warehouses). New total costs = ~$8.7M, new profit = ~$6.3M, new margin ~42%.

math.setup: Apply each expected percentage change to the current cost line, sum the new costs, recalculate profit and margin.
math.answer: New profit margin is approximately 42%, up from 20%.

recommendation: FC should consolidate its distribution network from 6 regional warehouses to primarily its North Carolina manufacturing site, retaining minimal warehouse presence only where necessary.
FC should partner with an overnight carrier (FedEx or UPS) using white-glove service ($150/set) to ship directly from the manufacturing site to retailers, matching the competitor's delivery model.
This restructuring is projected to reduce total costs from $12M to approximately $8.7M, improving profit margin from 20% to approximately 42%.
risks: Transition risk: coordinating the shift to a new logistics model without disrupting the current next-day delivery promise to upscale retailers.
Dependence on a third-party carrier (FedEx/UPS) for a premium, fragile product — any carrier service failures directly damage brand reputation.
White-glove carrier cost ($150/set) could rise; FC should negotiate long-term contracts.
Eliminating warehouses may reduce flexibility if demand ever spikes regionally.
next_steps: Negotiate white-glove overnight shipping contracts with FedEx and UPS.
Develop a phased warehouse consolidation plan, starting with the most distant/costly locations (Southern California, then Ohio).
Establish service-level agreements with the carrier to protect the next-day delivery promise.
Monitor per-set shipping costs closely vs. the $150/set assumption to validate the margin improvement.
